item.title: The Hormone Problem That Can Look Like 'Just Getting Older'
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Endocrine disease is one of the most common chronic health issues in middle-aged and senior pets, and because the signs develop so gradually, it is also one of the most frequently missed and misattributed to "just getting older"
  • The most common conditions are hypothyroidism in dogs, hyperthyroidism in senior cats, diabetes in both species, Cushing's disease in older dogs, and the less common but more dangerous Addison's disease
  • Hormones and the immune system are deeply intertwined — a sluggish thyroid or stressed adrenal gland can affect how well the body regulates inflammation and responds to challenges, making endocrine health part of the bigger immune picture
  • Watch for weight changes without diet changes, increased thirst or urination, coat or skin changes, excessive panting in dogs, or a senior cat losing weight despite eating ravenously — especially when two or three signs cluster together
  • Ask your veterinarian for a full thyroid panel including free T4 and thyroid autoantibody testing rather than a basic screen, and consider twice-yearly senior wellness bloodwork to catch hormonal shifts long before they show up in behavior

Your dog has slowed down a little. Their coat seems duller than it used to be. They have put on a few pounds without eating more. Or you might notice your senior cat is suddenly ravenous but losing weight, pacing more than usual, drinking from every water bowl in the house.

For a lot of pet parents, the easy explanation is "well, they are getting older." And sometimes they are. But sometimes those slow, drifting changes are actually a hormone problem — one that can be managed, often very well, if someone thinks to look for it.

Endocrine disease is one of the most common chronic health issues in middle-aged and senior pets, and it is also one of the most frequently missed. The signs develop so gradually that they are easy to attribute to normal aging, and the symptoms often overlap with half a dozen other conditions. Learning what to notice — and what to ask your vet about — is one of the more valuable things you can do for an older dog or cat.

The Endocrine System in Plain Terms

The endocrine system is your pet's hormone communication network. It is a set of glands — the thyroid in the neck, the adrenal glands near the kidneys, the pancreas between the stomach and small intestine, the pituitary at the base of the brain, the ovaries or testes, and the parathyroids overlying the thyroid gland — that release chemical messengers into the bloodstream to control metabolism, growth, stress response, blood sugar, calcium balance, and reproduction.1,2

These glands do not work in isolation. They constantly communicate with the immune system, the gut, the brain, and the nervous system. Because hormones travel throughout the body and each affects multiple organs, a problem in one small gland can produce symptoms that look at first like they belong to an entirely different system. When one gland drifts out of balance, the others tend to feel it — which is why a pet with an ongoing hormone issue often shows more than one symptom at a time.

The Most Common Endocrine Conditions

A few hormonal conditions turn up over and over in middle-aged and senior pets. They are not rare, they are not exotic, and most veterinarians recognize them quickly once they know to look. What makes them tricky is that each one tends to present as a cluster of small, slow-building changes rather than a single dramatic symptom — exactly the kind of pattern that gets written off as aging until bloodwork tells a different story. Here are the ones most worth knowing:3,4,5

  • Hypothyroidism in dogs — An underactive thyroid is common in middle-aged dogs. Signs include unexplained weight gain, hair loss or thinning coat, low energy, cold intolerance, and skin changes. A blood test confirms the diagnosis, and daily medication usually manages it well.
  • Hyperthyroidism in cats — The opposite problem shows up most often in senior cats. The thyroid becomes overactive — usually due to a benign enlargement or tumor — and speeds up the metabolism. The classic pattern is a cat that is losing weight despite eating ravenously, often restless, sometimes with a faster heartbeat, increased thirst, or a scruffy, greasy-looking coat. Treatment options include daily medication, a specialized diet, surgery, or radioactive iodine therapy.
  • Diabetes mellitus — This affects both dogs and cats when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or when the body stops responding to it properly. Signs include excessive thirst and urination, weight loss despite good appetite, and increasing lethargy. Signs may also include cataract formation (primarily in dogs) and abnormal posture and ability to walk (particularly in cats). With daily insulin and consistent diet management, most diabetic pets can live long, comfortable lives. Some cats can even go into diabetic remission.
  • Cushing's disease — Caused by excess cortisol stemming most often from a tumor on the pituitary gland or less often a tumor on the adrenal gland, it is most common in older dogs. Cushing’s can also be iatrogenic, meaning it is caused by long-term steroid administration. The classic picture includes a pot-bellied appearance, thinning skin that bruises and tears easily, hair loss, ravenous appetite, dramatically increased thirst and urination, and excessive panting. It develops so gradually that many owners mistake it for normal aging until a veterinarian notices the pattern. Diagnosis involves blood testing and sometimes abdominal imaging; treatment is usually long-term medication to control cortisol levels, but may involve surgery. In iatrogenic cases, treatment involves slowly weaning the pet off steroid therapy.
  • Addison's disease — This is the opposite problem, wherein the adrenal glands produce too little cortisol. It is less common than Cushing's but more dangerous because an untreated Addisonian crisis can cause critical electrolyte imbalances and a sudden, life-threatening drop in blood pressure. Sudden collapse, severe weakness, or vomiting in a dog, particularly with any history of adrenal disease or long-term steroid use, should be treated as an emergency.

The Signs That Are Not Just Aging

Because the connections between hormones and daily life are not obvious, the drift is easy to miss. Keep an eye out for:6,7

  • Weight change in either direction without a change in diet or activity
  • Marked increase in thirst and urination — not just a hot day
  • Coat changes — thinning, dullness, slow regrowth, greasy or unkempt texture
  • Skin that seems thinner or bruises more easily
  • Low energy or, in cats, unusual restlessness
  • Pot-bellied appearance and/or ravenous appetite in an older dog
  • A senior cat eating ravenously but still losing weight
  • Hair loss, especially symmetrical patches on the trunk
  • Excessive panting without obvious heat or exertion
  • Mood changes — new irritability, anxiety, or withdrawal without an obvious cause

Any one of these on its own might be nothing. But when two or three show up together, and they have been quietly building for weeks or months, that is exactly the pattern that points toward a hormone issue worth testing for.

The Hormone-Immune Connection

One piece integrative and holistic veterinarians talk about more than conventional practitioners do: hormones and the immune system are deeply intertwined. The endocrine and immune systems share signaling pathways, which means a hormone imbalance — especially involving the thyroid or adrenal glands — can change how well the immune system regulates inflammation and responds to challenges. A sluggish thyroid does not just mean a tired pet. It can mean an immune system that is not getting the metabolic support it needs to do its job well.

Autoimmune thyroiditis is a specific example — a condition where the immune system itself attacks the thyroid gland. This is why integrative veterinarians often recommend a full thyroid panel (including free T4 and thyroid autoantibody testing) rather than just a basic total T4 screen. The difference can be the difference between catching the issue early and missing it for years.

Chronic Stress and the HPA Axis

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is your pet's built-in stress response system. When something stressful happens, the brain signals the adrenal glands to release cortisol, which helps the body respond. Once the stress passes, the system should reset.8

The problem is when stress does not let up. Chronic pain, digestive problems, environmental instability, or any ongoing source of discomfort can keep the stress response switched on indefinitely. Research in dogs has found that prolonged activation of the stress response and elevated cortisol can affect immune function. Managing stress — through a predictable routine, calm handling, adequate sleep, and reducing avoidable stressors — supports both hormonal and immune health in ways that are easy to underestimate.

A Word on Testing

Endocrine conditions are confirmed through bloodwork, not guesswork, because the outward signs overlap heavily with other diseases. If your pet is showing any combination of the signs above, the right conversation with your vet is specific: ask about a full thyroid panel including free T4 and thyroid autoantibody testing, not just a basic screening. Ask about an ACTH stimulation test or low-dose dexamethasone suppression if Cushing's or Addison's is suspected. Ask about urine glucose and fructosamine if diabetes is on the table.

Senior pets benefit enormously from annual or, ideally, twice-yearly wellness bloodwork — not because something is necessarily wrong, but because many endocrine shifts show up in bloodwork long before they show up in behavior. Catching them early expands your options dramatically.

Nutrition and Lifestyle Foundations

Whole-food, species-appropriate nutrition gives the endocrine system the raw materials it needs. The thyroid depends on adequate iodine; selenium plays a role in converting thyroid hormone to its active form. Zinc and vitamin A, found in organ meats, support thyroid conversion and immune signaling. Protein quality matters because hormone production depends on amino acids. Feeding whole foods rather than highly processed foods helps to maintain a healthy gut microbiome and strong blood-intestine barrier, which reduces overall inflammation and provides a positive impact on the endocrine system.

A diet built around identifiable whole-food protein sources gives the endocrine system more to work with than one built around vague processed meat.9 Beyond diet, the simple factors add up, such as:

  • A quiet, consistent sleep space
  • Reduced environmental toxin load
  • Filtered water
  • Regular gentle exercise
  • Stress reduction
  • Avoiding unnecessary medications where possible

Some integrative veterinarians also use adaptogenic herbs to support adrenal function in specific pets — these should be chosen and dosed with veterinary guidance, not picked off a shelf.

When to Call the Vet

A routine appointment is appropriate for gradual weight change, a slightly duller coat, or mildly increased thirst that has been present for a week or more without other symptoms.

Same-day evaluation is warranted for marked increases in thirst and urination, especially paired with weight loss or lethargy — untreated diabetes and thyroid disease progress and get harder to manage over time.

Emergency care is needed for a pet that collapses, seems severely weak, vomits repeatedly, or shows an unsteady gait — particularly if there is any known history of Addison's disease or long-term steroid use. An adrenal crisis can be fatal within hours. Diabetic pets that stop eating, vomit, or become unusually weak may be developing a dangerous complication like diabetic ketoacidosis and need same-day attention. Any pet with a known endocrine condition that suddenly seems much worse than their baseline should be evaluated the same day.

Not Just Getting Older

The hard part about endocrine disease is that it hides in plain sight. Weight changes drift in over months. Coat quality dulls so slowly nobody notices until an old photo brings it into focus. Energy fades a little at a time, and the dog who used to insist on three walks a day gradually becomes the dog who is content with one. Any of that could be aging. Some of it almost certainly is. But some of it may be a hormone imbalance that is genuinely treatable — and left alone, it tends to worsen rather than plateau.

The next time your pet’s veterinary visit comes around, bring a list. Note the weight you remember from a year ago and the weight today. Note how much you are refilling the water bowl now versus six months ago. Note any coat or energy changes you have seen. Ask about a full thyroid panel rather than a basic screen if anything on your list rings a bell. In senior pets especially, those small observations become the raw material for catching hormonal issues before they do real damage. And once a diagnosis is made, most endocrine conditions in dogs and cats are manageable — often very well — for the rest of their lives.

Your old friend may not actually be "just getting older." They may be telling you something quieter, and more fixable, than that.

Sources and References

  • 1,3,7 United Pet Club, Endocrine system
  • 2,4,6,8,9 Dr. Ruth Roberts, The Endocrine-Immune Connection: Why Hormones Matter for Your Pet's Immune Health
  • 5 Saltwater Animal Hospital, Understanding Endocrinology in Dogs and Cats

item.title: Parrot Throws a Fit When Mom Turns Off Elmo
item.description:
Cruz watched Sesame Street once and immediately became Elmo's biggest fan. Now this hilarious parrot wakes Mom up asking for Elmo, refuses to let anyone change the channel, and gets upset when the TV goes off. His family may be tired of Elmo, but Cruz never will!

item.title: Fatal Tick-Borne Disease on the Rise in 17 US States
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Tick-borne illness is more common in dogs than cats, but cats do occasionally acquire tick-related diseases
  • One deadly tick-borne disease that is seen only in felines and is on the rise is cytauxzoonosis, which has now been confirmed in domestic cats in 17 U.S. states in the midwest and southeast
  • The first signs of infection include fever, lethargy and loss of appetite, which will be followed quickly by more serious symptoms such as difficulty breathing and jaundice
  • Cytauxzoonosis is often fatal, however, prompt treatment with a specific drug protocol and supportive care will give your pet the best chance for survival
  • Since the disease is so often fatal, it’s best to keep cats in tick endemic areas indoors, at least during tick season; cats who go outside should be carefully supervised and checked for ticks daily

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 25, 2017.

When people think about the problem of ticks and pets, they're more often concerned about tick-borne illnesses in dogs; however, ticks can and do latch onto kitties as well and transmit disease. Ticks attach to live animals because they need to ingest blood to survive and develop from larvae to adulthood. Larvae need blood to become nymphs; nymphs need blood to mature into adulthood; and adult female ticks need blood in order to mate and lay eggs.

Ticks in the nymph or adult stage pose the greatest risk for pets. Given the chance, the tick will attach to your cat's body and begin feeding on her blood. If the tick also happens to be carrying an infectious agent, it will be transmitted to your kitty, enter the circulatory system and begin to rapidly reproduce.

Now for some good news: Most ticks don't carry disease and most cats never acquire a tick-borne disease. In addition, kitties are very aware of even the tiniest pests on their bodies, and often will remove a tick before it has a chance to attach.

However, since occasionally veterinarians do see tick-borne illnesses in feline patients, it's a good idea for cat parents to be alert and aware. According to feline specialist Dr. Elizabeth Colleran, writing for veterinary journal dvm360, one tick-related disease that is on the increase in cats is cytauxzoonosis.1

Cytauxzoonosis is a disease resulting from the bite of a tick infected with the blood parasite Cytauxzoon felis. Bobcats are the primary hosts of C. felis, thus the nickname "bobcat fever," and when a tick feeds on an infected bobcat, it acquires the parasite.

If the infected tick then attaches to your cat, the pathogen can be transmitted to your kitty. The ticks most likely to carry the infection are the lone star tick and the American dog tick. All cats are considered susceptible to cytauxzoonosis, but interestingly, the infection has never been reported in any other species.

Cytauxzoonosis Is One of the Worst Tick-Borne Diseases Your Cat Can Get

In bobcats, cytauxzoonosis seems to cause only short-term illness, however, the animals do become "persistent carriers" of the disease. In domestic cats, the infection leads to severe illness and is often life-threatening. The C. felis parasite infects both the blood and tissues of cats. In a destructive process that takes about three weeks from the time of infection, the kitty will ultimately hemorrhage and die.

Infected ticks feed on the blood of bobcats, drop off, molt to their next life stage and attach to their next host. If the next host happens to be a domestic cat, a cytauxzoonosis infection can be the result. Fortunately, since the only way your cat can acquire cytauxzoonosis is through the bite of an infected tick that has fed on an infected bobcat, the disease is relatively rare.

The first reported case of cytauxzoonosis was in Missouri in 1976, but the geographic range has progressively expanded. As of this writing, cytauxzoonosis has been confirmed in domestic cats in 17 states, primarily in the midwest and southeast.

The pathogen has also been discovered in bobcats (but not yet in domestic kitties) in two additional states. Colleran recommends that veterinarians practicing in areas of the country where there are lone star ticks but no cytauxzoonosis reports yet, which includes much of the northeast and central U.S., be aware of the potential for the disease in feline patients.

Symptoms, Treatment, and Prognosis

Cats who spend time outdoors in areas where the disease has been reported are obviously at greatest risk for acquiring the infection. Initial symptoms include:

  • Fever
  • Lethargy
  • Loss of appetite
  • Rapid breathing and heart rate

Within days the kitty will experience severe weakness, jaundice, difficulty breathing and neurologic problems. Sadly, the disease is often fatal, but if treatment is given early enough, some cats do pull through. Your veterinarian can diagnose the disease with blood smears and PCR testing.

A drug protocol that has shown to improve survival rates (to about 60%) involves combining an antifungal/antiparasitic and an antibiotic. Supportive care should also be given in the form of intravenous (IV) fluids and blood thinners. Some kitties also require a feeding tube.

Integrative vets also treat these patients with ozone therapy, hyperbaric oxygen treatments and natural antimicrobial defense herbs (used in human tick borne infections). It's important to know that cats who recover from cytauxzoonosis may still carry the parasite and can suffer a recurrence of the infection.

Preventing Cytauxzoonosis in Your Cat

Fortunately, while cats who recover from the disease can continue to transmit the pathogen to ticks that attach to their bodies, the infection cannot be spread through physical contact with an infected cat. Since cytauxzoonosis (and any tick-borne illness) has the potential to be fatal, it's recommended to avoid exposing your cat to ticks whenever possible. This can be accomplished by keeping him inside, and if he goes outside, it should be under your direct supervision.

If you do allow your cat outside, it should be for a walk with you on a harness and leash, or in a safe outdoor enclosure that he can't get out of, and other animals can't get into. During the warm summer months, it's important to brush your cat's coat regularly, at least daily if he's outside everyday, and search for ticks that might have attached to his body.

If you discover a tick attached to your cat, you need to remove it with tweezers or a specially designed tick removal tool. Wearing gloves to prevent touching the tick directly, and washing your hands afterwards, is also recommended. It’s important that you remove the entire tick, including the head, by applying steady pressure as you pull it out. Once it’s off, flush it down the toilet.

Then disinfect your cat’s skin with soapy water or diluted povidone iodine (Betadine). Applying a drop of colloidal silver to the bite is also recommended. Monitor the attachment site for the next few days. If you notice any irritation or inflammation of the skin, contact your veterinarian.

Applying topical chemical flea and tick preventives or collars containing toxic chemicals to any pet isn't recommended, but especially not cats due to their extreme sensitivity to many of these substances. And never, ever use a flea and tick product designed for dogs on your cat, as it can be fatal.

If your cat ventures outside regularly, especially if you live in an area where lone star or American dog ticks are prevalent, putting an all-natural, non-toxic, herbal pest repellent collar on him can provide an extra layer of protection. You can also consider sprinkling him with diatomaceous earth, avoiding the face and head.

  • One deadly tick-borne disease that is seen only in felines and is on the rise is cytauxzoonosis, which has now been confirmed in domestic cats in 17 U.S. states in the midwest and southeast
  • The first signs of infection include fever, lethargy and loss of appetite, which will be followed quickly by more serious symptoms such as difficulty breathing and jaundice
  • Cytauxzoonosis is often fatal, however, prompt treatment with a specific drug protocol and supportive care will give your pet the best chance for survival
  • Since the disease is so often fatal, it’s best to keep cats in tick endemic areas indoors, at least during tick season; cats who go outside should be carefully supervised and checked for ticks daily

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 25, 2017.

When people think about the problem of ticks and pets, they're more often concerned about tick-borne illnesses in dogs; however, ticks can and do latch onto kitties as well and transmit disease. Ticks attach to live animals because they need to ingest blood to survive and develop from larvae to adulthood. Larvae need blood to become nymphs; nymphs need blood to mature into adulthood; and adult female ticks need blood in order to mate and lay eggs.

Ticks in the nymph or adult stage pose the greatest risk for pets. Given the chance, the tick will attach to your cat's body and begin feeding on her blood. If the tick also happens to be carrying an infectious agent, it will be transmitted to your kitty, enter the circulatory system and begin to rapidly reproduce.

Now for some good news: Most ticks don't carry disease and most cats never acquire a tick-borne disease. In addition, kitties are very aware of even the tiniest pests on their bodies, and often will remove a tick before it has a chance to attach.

However, since occasionally veterinarians do see tick-borne illnesses in feline patients, it's a good idea for cat parents to be alert and aware. According to feline specialist Dr. Elizabeth Colleran, writing for veterinary journal dvm360, one tick-related disease that is on the increase in cats is cytauxzoonosis.1

Cytauxzoonosis is a disease resulting from the bite of a tick infected with the blood parasite Cytauxzoon felis. Bobcats are the primary hosts of C. felis, thus the nickname "bobcat fever," and when a tick feeds on an infected bobcat, it acquires the parasite.

If the infected tick then attaches to your cat, the pathogen can be transmitted to your kitty. The ticks most likely to carry the infection are the lone star tick and the American dog tick. All cats are considered susceptible to cytauxzoonosis, but interestingly, the infection has never been reported in any other species.

Cytauxzoonosis Is One of the Worst Tick-Borne Diseases Your Cat Can Get

In bobcats, cytauxzoonosis seems to cause only short-term illness, however, the animals do become "persistent carriers" of the disease. In domestic cats, the infection leads to severe illness and is often life-threatening. The C. felis parasite infects both the blood and tissues of cats. In a destructive process that takes about three weeks from the time of infection, the kitty will ultimately hemorrhage and die.

Infected ticks feed on the blood of bobcats, drop off, molt to their next life stage and attach to their next host. If the next host happens to be a domestic cat, a cytauxzoonosis infection can be the result. Fortunately, since the only way your cat can acquire cytauxzoonosis is through the bite of an infected tick that has fed on an infected bobcat, the disease is relatively rare.

The first reported case of cytauxzoonosis was in Missouri in 1976, but the geographic range has progressively expanded. As of this writing, cytauxzoonosis has been confirmed in domestic cats in 17 states, primarily in the midwest and southeast.

The pathogen has also been discovered in bobcats (but not yet in domestic kitties) in two additional states. Colleran recommends that veterinarians practicing in areas of the country where there are lone star ticks but no cytauxzoonosis reports yet, which includes much of the northeast and central U.S., be aware of the potential for the disease in feline patients.

Cats who spend time outdoors in areas where the disease has been reported are obviously at greatest risk for acquiring the infection. Initial symptoms include:

  • Fever
  • Lethargy
  • Loss of appetite
  • Rapid breathing and heart rate

Within days the kitty will experience severe weakness, jaundice, difficulty breathing and neurologic problems. Sadly, the disease is often fatal, but if treatment is given early enough, some cats do pull through. Your veterinarian can diagnose the disease with blood smears and PCR testing.

A drug protocol that has shown to improve survival rates (to about 60%) involves combining an antifungal/antiparasitic and an antibiotic. Supportive care should also be given in the form of intravenous (IV) fluids and blood thinners. Some kitties also require a feeding tube.

Integrative vets also treat these patients with ozone therapy, hyperbaric oxygen treatments and natural antimicrobial defense herbs (used in human tick borne infections). It's important to know that cats who recover from cytauxzoonosis may still carry the parasite and can suffer a recurrence of the infection.

Preventing Cytauxzoonosis in Your Cat

Fortunately, while cats who recover from the disease can continue to transmit the pathogen to ticks that attach to their bodies, the infection cannot be spread through physical contact with an infected cat. Since cytauxzoonosis (and any tick-borne illness) has the potential to be fatal, it's recommended to avoid exposing your cat to ticks whenever possible. This can be accomplished by keeping him inside, and if he goes outside, it should be under your direct supervision.

If you do allow your cat outside, it should be for a walk with you on a harness and leash, or in a safe outdoor enclosure that he can't get out of, and other animals can't get into. During the warm summer months, it's important to brush your cat's coat regularly, at least daily if he's outside everyday, and search for ticks that might have attached to his body.

If you discover a tick attached to your cat, you need to remove it with tweezers or a specially designed tick removal tool. Wearing gloves to prevent touching the tick directly, and washing your hands afterwards, is also recommended. It’s important that you remove the entire tick, including the head, by applying steady pressure as you pull it out. Once it’s off, flush it down the toilet.

Then disinfect your cat’s skin with soapy water or diluted povidone iodine (Betadine). Applying a drop of colloidal silver to the bite is also recommended. Monitor the attachment site for the next few days. If you notice any irritation or inflammation of the skin, contact your veterinarian.

Applying topical chemical flea and tick preventives or collars containing toxic chemicals to any pet isn't recommended, but especially not cats due to their extreme sensitivity to many of these substances. And never, ever use a flea and tick product designed for dogs on your cat, as it can be fatal.

If your cat ventures outside regularly, especially if you live in an area where lone star or American dog ticks are prevalent, putting an all-natural, non-toxic, herbal pest repellent collar on him can provide an extra layer of protection. You can also consider sprinkling him with diatomaceous earth, avoiding the face and head.

item.title: The Herb That Can Turn Zoomies Into Naptime
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Catnip (Nepeta cataria) is a perennial herb in the mint family, and its magic ingredient is nepetalactone — the compound that acts as a pheromone and triggers the brain's reward and pleasure pathways in roughly 60% to 70% of adult cats
  • Sniffing catnip tends to produce energetic zoomies and playful behavior, while eating catnip typically can have the opposite effect — calming, almost sedative, making it useful for both playtime and winding down
  • About 30% to 40% of cats do not respond to catnip because of genetics, and kittens under six months rarely react at all — but alternatives like silvervine (effective in roughly 79% of cats), Tatarian honeysuckle, and valerian root can fill the gap
  • Fresh catnip is more potent than dried, catnip sprays work best for cats prone to stomach upset, and sessions should be limited to two or three times per week to avoid desensitization
  • Beyond fun, catnip can help calm pre-vet-visit anxiety, encourage exercise in indoor cats, soothe digestion as a mild tea, repel insects, and even support minor first-aid applications

You have seen it a hundred times: Your normally dignified cat rolls onto their back in a cloud of catnip, kneads the air, rubs their face into the carpet, and even lets out a chirp or a drool. And just as suddenly, it is over, and they stroll off like nothing happened. One small pinch of a green herb, and your living room went from frenzied to peaceful in about 10 minutes.

Catnip is one of the most entertaining tools in a cat parent's toolkit — and one of the more scientifically interesting. Here is what it actually does, how to use it well, and what to try if your cat is one of the many who shrug at it entirely.

What Catnip Actually Is (and What It Does to Your Cat)

Catnip (Nepeta cataria) is a perennial herb in the mint family, native to Europe and parts of Asia and now growing wild across much of North America. It grows about 2 to 3 feet tall with soft, fuzzy green leaves and small purple-spotted white flowers,1 and it releases its characteristic aromatic scent most strongly when crushed. The oil in those leaves contains a compound called nepetalactone — and nepetalactone is the entire story behind the famous reaction.2

When your cat sniffs catnip, nepetalactone binds to receptors in the nasal lining and triggers the brain's reward and pleasure pathways via pheromone-like activity. The result, in roughly 60% to 70% of adult cats, is a short burst of what looks a lot like euphoria — rolling, rubbing the face and body against the source, vocalizing, drooling, kneading, chasing imaginary prey.

The effect typically lasts between five and 15 minutes. After that, your cat becomes temporarily immune, with a refractory period of about 30 minutes before the same response can be triggered again.3

Sniff vs. Eat — Two Different Effects

Here is an interesting fact most cat parents do not know: Sniffing and eating catnip can produce opposite effects. Sniffing lights up the olfactory system and tends to produce the energetic, playful, zoomie-driven response. Eating catnip, by contrast, tends to produce a calmer, almost sedative effect — think naptime instead of party mode. The ingested compounds may interact differently with the digestive tract than with the olfactory system, although some scientists believe the difference is that chewing the catnip volatizes a more potent dose of the nepetalactone into the mouth and therefore the scent receptors. Small amounts are perfectly safe to eat, though larger quantities can cause mild stomach upset.4,5

This is why the same catnip toy can trigger a wild rolling session one minute and a peaceful curl-up the next — it may depend partly on whether your cat is sniffing or munching.

Why Some Cats Do Not Respond

Sensitivity to catnip is actually genetic, and roughly 30% to 40% of adult cats simply do not have the gene that produces a response. Nothing is wrong with those cats. They are just not wired for it.

Kittens under three to six months rarely react either — the behavioral response usually does not emerge until closer to sexual maturity, generally around six months of age. If you have been trying catnip with a young kitten and getting zero reaction, that is completely normal.6,7

Alternatives Worth Trying

If your adult cat is a catnip non-responder, do not give up on the whole category. Several plants in other families create similar responses that can do the trick:8,9

  • Silvervine (Actinidia polygama) — Probably the most important alternative, most Western cat parents have not heard of. It has been used in Japan for centuries as a cat stimulant, where cats' reaction is called the Matatabi Dance. Studies have found about 79% of domestic cats respond positively, including many who are unmoved by catnip.
  • Tatarian honeysuckle wood — Effective in roughly half of cats. Comes in small wooden pieces that cats chew and drool on. Less tidy than catnip but satisfying for cats who enjoy it.
  • Valerian root — Less predictable, working in about 47% to 50% of cats, but the stimulant effect can be intense for those who respond. One warning: valerian smells strongly unpleasant to human noses.

Offer these systematically rather than all at once — introduce one, watch the response over a few days, then try the next if there is no interest.

Fresh, Dried, or Spray Form?

Fresh catnip is significantly more potent than the dried variety because the nepetalactone has not had time to volatilize. A small pinch of fresh herb will produce a stronger reaction than a larger amount of dried. If you have the space, growing a plant indoors on a sunny windowsill is easy, inexpensive, and gives you a perpetual supply. Treat it roughly like you would a basil plant.

Dried catnip is more practical for most households. Keep it in an airtight container away from heat to preserve potency. Sprinkle it on a toy, a scratching post, or a small piece of fabric sewn into a pouch.

Catnip sprays are the best choice for cats who get stomach upset from ingesting the herb — they deliver the olfactory trigger without any consumption. Sprays are also useful for refreshing old toys that have lost their appeal.

Beyond Fun — The Real Health Benefits

For a plant that is mostly associated with silly rolling and five-minute play sessions, catnip’s range of practical uses is surprisingly broad — enough that integrative and holistic veterinarians increasingly treat it as a real tool in a cat's wellness routine rather than just a novelty herb:10,11,12

  • Calming anxiety — For cats that get stressed before veterinary visits, car rides, or home renovations, a small amount of catnip 20 to 30 minutes beforehand can take the edge off. The post-euphoria phase tends to leave cats noticeably relaxed. Cats dealing with mild separation anxiety may benefit from a catnip-infused toy left out during your absence.
  • Encouraging exercise — For indoor cats who may not get enough physical activity, catnip-infused toys or scattered dried leaves can be an enticing motivator to play — which supports healthy weight, longevity, and overall well-being.
  • Digestive support — Catnip tea (brewed mild and cooled) has traditionally been used to soothe upset stomachs in cats, dogs, and people.
  • Natural insect repellent — Studies have found catnip oil to be a surprisingly powerful mosquito deterrent — some research has suggested it rivals DEET for repelling insects.
  • First-aid support — Catnip oil has antimicrobial properties and has been used topically for minor wounds and ear irritation in traditional applications.

That said, catnip is a tool, not a treatment. If your cat has persistent or severe anxiety, loop in your vet about a comprehensive plan rather than relying on catnip alone.

How Often Is Too Often

Overexposure to catnip leads to desensitization — the responses become weaker and shorter until eventually the cat stops reacting at all. To keep catnip effective, limit sessions to two or three times per week at most. Put catnip toys away between uses so they retain novelty. Think of it the way you would think of a special treat: valuable precisely because it is not always available.

The good news is that catnip is not addictive. Cats with unlimited access simply stop responding to it rather than developing any kind of dependency. However, make sure to keep these safety guidelines in mind:

  • Never force catnip on a cat who shows no interest — there is no benefit, only unnecessary stress
  • Avoid highly concentrated catnip essential oils, which can be overwhelming
  • Monitor first-time exposures — occasionally a cat becomes briefly overstimulated or even aggressive
  • If your cat vomits after eating catnip, switch to spray-only application
  • Choose organic, additive-free catnip to avoid pesticide residues on something your cat will roll in and lick
  • Start small — too much catnip can cause mild tummy upset

What About Dogs?

Some holistic pet retailers suggest catnip can benefit dogs — a sprinkle on food or a mild catnip tea for digestion and calming, or formulas that include catnip for stress support. However, other veterinary experts recommend keeping catnip away from dogs altogether because it can cause digestive upset, though it is not toxic to them.13,14

If you want to try catnip with your dog, start with a very small amount, watch closely for any digestive reaction, and talk to an integrative veterinarian about whether it is an appropriate addition to their calming routine. Dogs do not experience the sniff-driven euphoric response the way cats do, but the calmer, digestive-supporting applications may still work for some.

The Real Takeaway

Catnip is one of the genuinely enjoyable parts of living with a cat — a harmless, inexpensive, reliably entertaining ritual when used thoughtfully. Know your cat's response patterns. Keep sessions occasional enough that they stay meaningful. Pick good-quality organic catnip over mystery-source product. And if your particular cat is in the non-responsive 30% to 40%, do not take it personally — try silvervine or Tatarian honeysuckle, and you may discover an entirely new side of them.

Used well, catnip really can turn frantic zoomies into peaceful naptime. Just a tiny sprinkle, a toy flung across the room, and five to ten minutes of pure goofball joy — followed by the quiet contentment that makes living with a cat such a specific delight. There is not much else that costs almost nothing and delivers that much happiness in a single afternoon.

Sources and References

  • 1 Midwest Invasive Species Information Network, Catnip
  • 2,12 The Innocent Hound, The Ultimate Guide to Catnip: Exploring the Benefits of Catnip
  • 3,5,6,8,10,14 Independence Veterinary Clinic, August 3, 2023
  • 4,7,11,13 The Pet Beastro, March 21, 2025
  • 9 BMC Vet Res. 2017 Mar 16;13(1):70. doi: 10.1186/s12917-017-0987-6

item.title: Rejuvenating and Energizing for Your Older Pet — Sends Aches and Pains Packing
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Your senior or geriatric pet needs to stay active even though he's getting up in years
  • Exercises to help older pets stay mobile include passive-range-of-motion exercises, balance and proprioception exercises, and targeted strengthening exercises
  • Massage and gentle stretching are also helpful to keep muscles loose and toned, and ease the stiffness of arthritis
  • Chiropractic, acupuncture, water exercises for dogs and appropriate joint supplements can also be very beneficial for older pets
  • Short, frequent walks for dogs and daily interactive play sessions for cats help maintain heart health in older pets

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published May 26, 2018.

Just as humans need to stay active to fully enjoy their golden years, so do senior and geriatric cats and dogs. The process of getting older can trigger a bit of a vicious cycle, in that aging bodies lose muscle tone and balance, which can lead to inactivity.

Inactivity leads to weight gain and added stress on joints that are no longer well-supported by adequate muscle mass. Inactivity and loss of muscle mass/balance promotes faster aging, as well as significantly increased risk of injury from slips, trips, falls, strains and sprains. Fortunately, with your help your older pet can break the cycle and gain tremendous benefits from anti-aging activities, including:

  • Exercises specifically designed to maintain strength, flexibility and balance
  • Short, frequent walks with your dog or interactive play sessions with your cat to maintain heart health
  • Massage to relieve sore muscles and joints, and other aches and pains

Some activities require the expertise or guidance of an animal rehabilitation therapist, but others don’t, such as taking your older dog for several short walks each day to promote cardiovascular fitness, or committing to two or three 20-minute daily interactive play sessions with your senior kitty.

You can also learn how to do massage on your pet from your veterinarian, most animal rehab therapists or a professional small animal massage practitioner.

Exercises to Help Your Older Pet Stay Active

There are three types of exercises that are beneficial for aging bodies:

  • Passive range-of-motion (PROM) exercises
  • Exercises that maintain balance and fluid movement
  • Exercises that target the big, body-supporting muscles like the hamstrings and gluteals

Passive range-of-motion exercises

PROM exercises can benefit both incapacitated and physically healthy pets. They are performed on a pet who is lying on her side in a comfortable position. The limbs are gently flexed and extended one at a time. It's important to keep the leg's position parallel to the body wall to avoid torque on the joints. It's also important not to hyperextend the wrists or ankles.

Passive range-of-motion exercises include:

  • Forelimb flexion
  • Shoulder flexion + elbow extension
  • Hind limb flexion
  • Hip and stifle extension
  • Shoulder and elbow extension
  • Shoulder abduction
  • Hip flexion + stifle extension
  • Hip abduction

Balance and proprioception (spatial orientation and movement) exercises

These include the use of cookie stretches, which are exercises that help older pets remain flexible while also encouraging improved balance and physical stability. The cookie stretch starts with a dog in a standing position. The goal is to have her reach for the cookie without taking any steps. The cookie is offered from various angles to encourage stretching in different directions.

The dog is rewarded with the treat when she achieves the desired position. The exercise can be made more challenging by requiring the dog to hold the position for 10 to 30 seconds. Cookie stretch exercises include spinal extension, spinal dorsiflexion, lateral spinal flexion and lateral spinal flexion with rotation. Another exercise to improve balance, strength and flexibility involves either walking or high-stepping a pet over Cavaletti poles.

Targeted strengthening exercises

These exercises in older pets are designed to work the big muscle groups that help with standing, walking and running. The sidestepping exercise strengthens the glutes and lateral thigh muscles. Stand facing your dog's side, with one hand on her collar and one hand on the opposite hip. Step into your pet until she steps to the side with a lateral move, but no forward motion. item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Fresh or frozen, raspberries are delicious fruits that can offer myriad benefits for you and your pet, including banishing harmful free radicals, supporting heart health and even ease aging joints
  • They offer a wealth of inflammation-busting antioxidants, including vitamin C, as well as polyphenols like ellagitannins and anthocyanins
  • Raspberry polyphenols have a protective effect against arthritis. In a study that used mice models, researchers found that the mice group that was given raspberry extract had a lower incidence and severity of arthritis compared to the control group
  • Pet parents are worried about the natural xylitol content of this fruit. The good news is only trace amounts of this sweetener are found in raspberries, so there’s no real danger when you feed your pet a few pieces
  • When sharing raspberries with your pet by adding them to pet treats, make sure the treats only make up around 10% of your pet’s daily caloric intake

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published March 7, 2024.

Known as a “dessert fruit” for its various uses in sweet pastries and ice cream, raspberries (Rubus idaeus) are small fruits with a sweet, juicy taste and a tart undertone. While you’ll often see them red, they can also come in other colors like black, gold and purple.1 Raspberries are versatile and can be used for various dishes and can also be shared with your pet. Here’s what you should know about feeding these berries to your furry friend.

What Are Raspberries and How Can They Benefit Your Pet?

Raspberries are perennials that grow on bushes and thrive best in places with cool summers and mild winters.2 Although they’re called “berries,” technically they are an aggregate of what’s called “drupelets” — small fleshy fruits — that are clumped together.3 Fresh raspberries can be bought from June to October, but you can also find frozen varieties in groceries all year-round.4

Despite their small size, raspberries pack a lot of punch with nutrients, including vitamins, minerals and antioxidants that may help boost your pet’s well-being. Manganese,5 calcium and vitamin K,6 nutrients that play important roles in bone health, are all present in raspberries.

Whether fresh or frozen, these delicious fruits can offer myriad benefits for you and your pet, including banishing harmful free radicals,7 supporting heart health8 and easing aging joints.9

However, as with many other human foods, some pet parents have been misguided into thinking that raspberries can be dangerous to pets. Many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds are safe for pets to consume, despite the misinformation surrounding them on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of overconsumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has nevertheless managed to confuse millions of pet lovers.

In the case of raspberries, pet parents are worried about the natural xylitol content of this fruit. Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that’s used in many food products today, and with dogs, consuming it can lead to a sudden release of insulin, followed by a sharp drop in blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which can trigger vomiting, loss of consciousness and seizures.

The good news is only trace amounts of this sweetener are found in raspberries, meaning it’s not a high risk for danger if you feed your pet a few pieces.

Did You Know?

To receive a fatal dose of xylitol from raspberries, a 22-pound dog would have to eat 32 cups of raspberries. So as long as you give it in moderate amounts, you have nothing to worry about.10

Raspberries Are Rich in Antioxidants

“Raspberries offer a wealth of inflammation-busting antioxidants, including vitamin C, lutein and zeaxanthin, as well as polyphenols like ellagitannins and anthocyanins.”

Just 10 raspberries can provide as much as 4.98 milligrams of vitamin C, which may help increase the immunomodulating potential in healthy canines.11 While most mammals can actually synthesize vitamin C in their liver,12 having supplementary support may help improve their well-being.

Phytochemicals found in raspberries include ellagitannins and anthocyanins, polyphenols that have important benefits for pets. Ellagitannins offer some protection against illnesses like heart disease13 and cancer,14,15 while anthocyanins, which are flavonoid compounds responsible for the red and blue color in fruits, are found to cross the blood-brain barrier, and may have neurodegenerative and cognitive effects.16

Raspberry polyphenols may also have a protective effect against arthritis. In a study that used mice models, the anti-inflammatory properties of ellagitannins and anthocyanins were evaluated. They found that the mice that were given raspberry extract had a lower incidence and severity of arthritis compared to the control group.17

The flavonols in raspberries may also help inhibit different stages of tumor development, according to animal studies. A 2015 study published in the Food and Function journal found that red raspberries may help inhibit melanoma among mice subjects.18 According to a 2015 study in the Journal of Ophthalmology:19

"In these animal models, lutein and zeaxanthin have been reported to have beneficial effects in protecting ocular tissues and cells (especially the retinal neurons) against damage caused by different etiological factors.
The mechanisms responsible for these effects of lutein and zeaxanthin include prevention of phototoxic damage by absorption of blue light, reduction of oxidative stress through antioxidant activity and free radical scavenging, and their anti-inflammatory and antiangiogenic properties."

Raspberries Also Provide Enough Fiber for Your Pet’s Diet

Raspberries are included in the list of whole food sources with high amounts of dietary fiber,20 with 10 pieces of this fruit offering as much as 1.24 grams.21 While dogs and cats only need minimal amounts of fiber from their diet, getting it from vegetables and fruits like raspberries can help build their microbiome and provide roughage for optimal bowel health.

Soluble fiber in particular helps regulate bowel movements and gastric emptying. Hence, adding small amounts of fiber-rich foods like raspberries to your pet’s species-appropriate, nutritionally balanced diet can go a long way to boosting their well-being.22

Raspberries Fun Fact

According to Greek mythology, raspberries used to be white. When Ida, Zeus’s nursemaid, went out to pick the fruits, a thorn pricked her finger and ended up staining the raspberries. They have remained red ever since.23

How to Safely Feed Raspberries to Your Pets

Raspberries should be washed thoroughly before sharing with pets, making sure to remove the stems and leaves. Depending on your pet’s size, you may need to slice the berries into halves or quarters, so as not to pose a choking hazard. Here are some ideas on how to use raspberries:24

  • Add a few slices or mash them and put over your pet’s meal to make a healthy topper.
  • Blend raspberries with other pet-safe fruits and make a smoothie that you can smear all over their lick mat.
  • Stuff a few pieces into their favorite training toys for a fun activity.
  • Mix with some plain, organic yogurt for a refreshing treat.

When sharing raspberries with your pet by adding them to pet treats, make sure the treats only make up around 10% of your pet’s daily caloric intake.

Top Raspberry-Producing Countries in the World

According to 2021 statistics of 44 countries, Russia ranked first in terms of raspberry production, with 197,700 tons of this fruit harvested. Mexico and Serbia follow in second and third place, respectively.25

An Easy but Yummy Way to Let Your Pet Enjoy Raspberries

If you’re looking for a simple way to make healthy treats using raspberries, here’s a recipe you can try: Frozen Coconut and Berry Treats.26 Aside from fresh raspberries and blueberries, you can use other healthy fruits like blackberries or cranberries. Share this with your pet on hot days!

Frozen Coconut and Berry Treats Recipe

Ingredients:

  • Coconut oil
  • Berries or fruits of your choice (raspberries, blueberries or blackberries)

Procedure:

  1. Get the coconut oil to a liquid consistency.
  2. Wash your berries of choice and place in an ice tray.
  3. Add the coconut oil and allow to freeze for a few hours.

Let your pet enjoy these cool treats!

Are Raspberries Sustainable?

Compared to other types of food, raspberries have a fairly low carbon footprint, around 0.15 kilograms (0.33 pounds) of CO2e per pound. This is mainly due to their high-growth resources, such as land use, pesticides and irrigation. Overall, they are a carbon-conscious fruit, though some aspects of the production need to be considered, such as transportation and packaging — for example, they are usually wrapped in plastic and kept refrigerated during transport to great distances.27

Although they’re not on the EWG’s 2026 Dirty Dozen list,28 raspberries are sprayed by pesticides because they’re prone to pests and diseases,29 so make sure to buy organic, spray-free raspberries from your local markets.

After surviving an encounter with a cat, Pickle was nursed back to health and released into the wild. But she wasn't ready to say goodbye! For months, she returned at 7 a.m. for breakfast, neck scratches, and a bath before flying off on her next adventure.

item.title: Keep Your Pet Out of Harm's Way Till Fully Protected from These Robust Bugs
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • There are many contagious diseases dogs can contract from other dogs, and among them are parvo, distemper, infectious hepatitis and rabies
  • These four diseases are very serious and fatal, and every effort should be made to prevent them
  • Your pet can and should be protected from these diseases through a series of well-timed puppy shots, followed by titer tests to confirm immunity
  • Until your puppy is fully immunized, it’s important to be very cautious if you take him to places where other dogs congregate
  • Parvo is a hardy virus that can survive in the environment for long periods and spread on a dog's hair, feet, shoes and contaminated objects

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published January 10, 2018.

Certain diseases that affect dogs are the result of factors such as lifestyle (for example, obesity and diabetes) and genetics (e.g., brachycephalic airway syndrome in breeds with pushed-in faces such as Pugs), and there is a wealth of information here at Mercola Healthy Pets on how lifestyle and genetics influence your pet's health.

But the topic today is contagious diseases your canine companion can acquire from other dogs, and specifically the life-threatening diseases every puppy should be vaccinated against: parvovirus, distemper, infectious hepatitis and rabies.

4 Contagious and Fatal Canine Diseases

  1. Parvovirus — Canine parvovirus type 2, or CPV-2, is a virus that attacks the gastrointestinal (GI) tract of both domesticated and wild puppies and adult dogs. In addition to the gastrointestinal effects of parvo, in very young and unborn puppies, it can damage the heart muscle as well.

    Parvo is extremely contagious and is passed by direct dog-to-dog contact and contact with contaminated feces, environments and people. The virus can contaminate everything your dog touches, food and water bowls, collars and leashes, and the people who handle your dog and their clothing.

    Parvo is a hardy virus that can survive extremes in temperature and humidity levels. It lives in the environment for long periods of time. Even tiny amounts of parvo-infected stool can contaminate an area and transmit the disease to other dogs entering the area. Parvo can be easily spread from one location to another on a dog's hair or feet, on a contaminated pet carrier and on shoes and other objects.
  2. Distemper — Canine distemper, which is also known as Carre's disease and was once called hard pad disease, is a highly contagious virus that primarily affects young dogs, both domesticated and wild, between the ages of 2 and 6 months. The disease can be fatal, especially in puppies and wildlife.

    Non-immunized dogs that come in contact with an infected animal carry a high risk of contracting distemper, as do puppies born to an infected mother, and young dogs under extreme stress or who are immunocompro­mised. Dogs exposed to wildlife may also have a heightened risk of contracting the disease.

    Bacterial infections, especially of the respiratory or GI tract may also make dogs more susceptible to the virus. On rare occasions, improperly attenuated (formulated) CDV vaccines have also been implicated as a cause.

    However, most dogs are exposed to the virus that when they inhale the respiratory secretions of an infected animal, or come in direct contact with infected feces, urine or saliva. CDV can also be spread through direct or indirect contact with the bedding, bowls or other items belonging to an infected dog.

    In susceptible dogs, the virus first reproduces in the respiratory tract and then moves on to the lymph nodes and the lymph and blood circulatory systems throughout the body. CDV can also infect a dog's skin, GI and urogenital tracts, central nervous system and other areas of the body. Infected dogs can shed the virus for several months after infection, even when they are not showing clinical signs of illness.
  3. Infectious hepatitis — Infectious canine hepatitis, or ICH, is caused by the canine adenovirus type 1 (CAV-1). The infection can cause damage to cells throughout a dog's body, especially those located in the liver, kidneys and eyes. At one time, there was a vaccine available to protect dogs from type 1 adenovirus, but it was discontinued because it caused a condition called blue eye, which is a protein deposit that resulted in a bluish tint to one or both eyes of vaccinated dogs.

    These days, dogs are vaccinated against canine adenovirus type 2 (CAV-2), which is a kennel cough virus, and the same core vaccine provides cross-protection against canine adenovirus type 1 as well.

    ICH is found all over the world, and is spread by bodily fluids, including nasal discharge and urine. The most common method of transmission is direct contact with an infected dog, especially the dog's urine. Contami­nated kennels or living quarters, bowls and other supplies, and human hands and shoes can also transmit the virus.

    Dogs that recover from infectious canine hepatitis can shed the virus for up to a year in urine, which makes it very difficult to determine exactly what locations might be contaminated.

    The infectious particles enter a dog's body through the nose or mouth and invade the tonsils, where the virus replicates and then infects nearby lymph nodes. The cytotoxic particles spread from the lymphatic system to the bloodstream in about a week. Once travelling through the blood, the virus infects other target organs, including the liver, kidneys and eyes, with the liver almost always being the most severely affected organ.
  4. Rabies — The rabies virus, also called acute viral encephalomyelitis, is an extremely serious, usually fatal inflammatory infection that affects the brain and central nervous system (CNS). In dogs (and cats) in the U.S., the rabies virus is most often transmitted when an infected fox, raccoon, skunk, coyote or bat bites a pet. Infectious virus particles are present in the saliva of these animals to more efficiently transmit the disease.

    It's extremely rare, but transmission has also been documented to occur through exposure to the escaping gases of an infected decomposing animal. This form of transmission usually occurs in caves where there are large populations of infected bats. It's something to think about if you have a hunting dog or you like to explore caves with your dog.

    Rabies is a zoonotic disease, meaning it can also be transmitted to humans by infected animals. Once the rabies virus enters a pet's body, it multiplies in muscle cells, and then spreads to nearby peripheral sensory and motor nerves, which move it to the brain and central nervous system (CNS).

    During the incubation period before the virus enters the CNS, the infected animal doesn't exhibit symptoms and can't transmit the disease. The virus moves relatively slowly, with the average time between exposure to brain involvement being three to eight weeks in dogs. However, incubation periods as long as six months have been reported in dogs.

Responsible Immunization Keeps Your Dog Safe from These Contagious, Often Fatal Diseases

Many pet parents are against all veterinary vaccines. And many vaccines conventional veterinarians recommend do provide more risk than benefit, in particular bacterin-based vaccines and non-core vaccines. But in some situations, leaving your puppy unvaccinated poses a much greater risk than benefit (those of you working in shelters and rescues know exactly what this means).

It’s important to understand that not vaccinating your pet against the four diseases discussed above means he’s unprotected from infection. He’ll be safe if you never let him outdoors or socialize him, which is obviously unthinkable. Your dog is a social creature — you can’t isolate him and expect a good outcome.

Dogs deserve to go outside, run, breathe fresh air, move their bodies through the woods, sniff things and interact with other dogs. However, all these behaviors pose a risk to their health if they aren't protected against highly contagious, deadly diseases. Over-vaccination is a terrible problem in the veterinary community, but in my professional opinion, providing baseline protection against these four diseases provides your pet with lifetime immunity — and you with peace of mind.

The Recommended Core Vaccine Protocol

The vaccine protocol for puppies is to administer a first round of distemper, parvo and adenovirus before 12 weeks of age, usually around 9 to 10 weeks. The second round is given between 15 and 16 weeks. Two weeks after the second round, titering is done to insure the dog has been immunized and not just vaccinated.

When it comes to rabies, the first vaccine is preferably given at 6 months, and then as required by law, a booster one year later and every three years thereafter. Until immunity is established through titering at the two- to four-week mark after your pup's second round of shots, use extreme care if you take her to places where other dogs congregate, including:

  • Pet stores
  • Dog parks
  • Puppy or obedience classes
  • Doggy daycare or boarding facilities
  • Grooming shops

Also, don't let your dog of any age come in contact with the poop of other dogs or wild animals, and properly dispose of your own pet's poop as well. If your dog is vomiting or has diarrhea or has been exposed to an ill dog, keep him away from any area where he might come in contact with other dogs or wild animals.

Unvaccinated dogs should not be exposed to ill dogs or those with questionable health or immunization histories. And if you are in contact with a sick dog, avoid contact with other dogs until you've washed your hands thoroughly and changed clothes, if necessary.

Sources and References

  • PetMD, August 3, 2016

item.title: Is Your Old Friend Trying to Catch Their Breath?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • November is Senior Pet Care Awareness Month, which makes it the perfect time to check your pet’s breathing, and loop in your vet at the first subtle change
  • A healthy dog at rest breathes between 15 and 30 times per minute — anything consistently above 30 at rest (laying down quietly or sleeping) in a cool and calm environment, is outside the normal range and warrants attention
  • Heart disease is the leading cause of respiratory difficulty in older dogs, with veterinary cardiology estimating up to 10% of dogs in general practice have some form of heart disease, especially older small breed dogs
  • Tracheal collapse is a common cause in older small breed dogs causing coughing after excitement or after drinking water
  • Red flags for immediate emergency care include blue, purple, or white gums, open-mouth breathing at rest, extended-neck posture, collapse, or coughing up pink frothy fluid

November is Senior Pet Care Awareness Month, which makes this the right moment to pay attention to changes in your senior pets. One of the most important signals the body can send is rapid or labored breathing — unfortunately, it’s also one of the easiest to brush off as "just aging."

Breathing changes in a senior dog are a red flag. They point to conditions that are often treatable when caught early, but dangerous when left alone. Keep reading to learn more.

Why Age Changes the Breathing Picture

Your dog's heart, lungs, and vascular system all experience some degree of functional decline with age. Conditions that accumulate and worsen over years, like heart valve disease, pulmonary fibrosis, chronic anemia, and laryngeal nerve degeneration, become far more prevalent in older dogs and the first sign may be changes in breathing. A 7-year-old dog breathing faster than usual is more likely to have an underlying medical cause than a 2-year-old dog, and the range of explanations are broader and more serious.1

The same change in a younger dog might just be excitement or anxiety. In an older dog, it's a signal worth investigating. And because the systems involved — heart, lungs, airways, and circulatory system — tend to decline gradually rather than suddenly, the earliest signs are often subtle enough that a pet parent might shrug them off. So, if your senior dog is breathing differently, there's usually a reason.

What Normal Looks Like

A healthy dog at rest breathes between 15 and 30 times per minute.2 Anything consistently above 30 at rest, in a cool and calm environment, is outside the normal range and warrants attention. Counting your dog's breaths per minute while they're settled is one of the most useful numbers you can give your vet.

Beyond rate, the character of breathing matters. Normal breathing is quiet, effortless, and rhythmic. Breathing that's audibly labored, accompanied by visible chest or abdominal movement, extended neck posture, open mouth at rest, or unusual sounds like wheezing, crackling, roaring, or rasping is abnormal regardless of the rate. If you are concerned it may help to take a video of your pet’s breathing — including how their chest is moving and abnormal neck posture or coughing — to show your vet.

The Common Culprits in Senior Dogs

A handful of conditions show up repeatedly in older dogs with breathing changes. Knowing them helps you connect what you're seeing to what might be going on:3,4

  • Heart disease — The leading cause of respiratory difficulty in older dogs. Veterinary cardiology estimates that up to 10% of dogs seen in general practice have some form of heart disease, with older small breed dogs at highest risk.5 As the heart's ability to pump efficiently declines, fluid can accumulate in the lungs (pulmonary edema), restricting oxygen exchange. Signs include a soft cough that gradually worsens, reduced exercise tolerance, a cough that wakes your dog from sleep, and reluctance to lie flat or on their back (dogs often sleep sitting up or in a position that opens their chest).
  • Tracheal collapse — This is a common condition that affects mostly small breed dogs including Pomeranians, Chihuahuas, Toy Poodles, and Yorkshire Terriers, as well as many other breeds. It often worsens with age as the tracheal cartilage deteriorates. The classic sign is a goose-honk cough triggered by excitement, pulling on a collar, or drinking water. There is herbal therapy available to treat this as well as supplements to support the tracheal cartilage and medication for severe cases.
  • Laryngeal paralysis — Another common cause of breathing changes, this is particularly common in large breeds such as Labrador Retrievers and Lab mixes. The arytenoid cartilages that normally open the airway during inhalation become paralyzed due to degeneration of nerves and stay partly closed. The telltale sound is loud, raspy, honking, or roaring inhalation.

    Dogs may become reluctant to exercise, gag, and bring up foamy liquid — and some may even develop aspiration pneumonia. Symptoms may worsen in warm or humid weather. In advanced cases, the gums can turn blue from oxygen deprivation. Treatment options include acupuncture treatment for mild cases as well as surgery to “tie back” the paralyzed cartilage and open the airway.6
  • Respiratory infections and pneumonia — These can be caused by exposure to bacteria or viruses that cause respiratory infections in any age dogs and can be assessed with an oral or nasal PCR test. A chest X-ray will look for conditions such as bronchitis or pneumonia. Aspiration pneumonia can also develop from aspirated food or liquid, or inhaled foreign material. Symptoms include coughing, nasal discharge, and rapid or labored breathing that needs prompt treatment. It is treatable with antibiotics and herbal therapy, although severe cases may need supplemental oxygen and IV medication.
  • Lung tumors or metastatic cancer — More common in older dogs. Tumors in the chest cavity, whether primary or spread from elsewhere, can impair breathing as they grow. They can cause a cough, exercise intolerance, or breathing difficulty.
  • Pleural effusion — Fluid accumulates around the lungs rather than inside them, compressing the space available for breathing. Most cases stem from underlying heart disease, but this may also be caused by a mass on the heart or in the chest. Dogs with pleural effusion are often reluctant to lie down and more comfortable sitting or standing.
  • Chronic bronchitis and pulmonary fibrosis — Chronic bronchitis causes persistent airway inflammation and mucus production — it may be due to underlying allergies or inflammation. Pulmonary fibrosis — which can result from previous heartworm infection damage or may be hereditary in certain breeds (West Highland White Terriers) causes scarring of lung tissue that limits oxygen exchange. Both lead to gradual-onset increased breathing effort and persistent cough.
  • Pain — An often-overlooked driver. Arthritis flares, abdominal discomfort, post-surgical recovery, or any significant pain can increase breathing rate and panting through the body's stress response. Watch for restlessness, difficulty finding a comfortable position, or sensitivity to touch alongside the breathing change.
  • Anemia — Reduced red blood cells mean reduced oxygen delivery, so the body compensates by breathing faster. Pale or whitish gums (instead of healthy pink) are a key indicator. It may be due to an underlying autoimmune disease, internal bleeding, or chronic kidney disease. A blood test is required for diagnosis.
  • Cognitive dysfunction and anxiety — Senior dogs with cognitive decline may feel confused and frightened — particularly at night — leading to panting, pacing, and faster breathing when the house is quiet and environmental cues are limited.
  • Cushing's disease and other hormonal conditions — Cushing's (overproduction of cortisol) is one of the more common endocrine disorders in middle-aged and senior dogs. It can cause persistent panting alongside a pot-bellied appearance, increased appetite, thirst, and urination, and in severe cases hair loss or skin changes. Thyroid issues and diabetes can also change breathing patterns.
  • Medication side effects — Corticosteroids are a common culprit for new-onset panting. If breathing changes started after a new prescription, mention it to your vet.

The Red Flags That Can't Wait

Some signs mean you need to get to a vet immediately. If you see any of the following, skip the waiting-to-see-what-happens step and head to an emergency clinic or call your vet for immediate guidance:7,8

  • Blue, purple, gray, or white-tinged gums (severe oxygen deprivation).
  • Open-mouth breathing while at rest — dogs are obligate nasal breathers at rest, so this is a serious signal.
  • Breathing more than forty times per minute at rest that doesn't slow after calm rest in a cool environment.
  • Extended neck posture, flared nostrils, elbows pushed out from the body, or “abdominal breathing” — visible movement of the whole chest and abdomen with each breath.
  • Sudden onset in a dog who was previously breathing normally, especially with collapse or extreme weakness.
  • Coughing up pink frothy fluid or any blood.
  • Reluctance or inability to lie down comfortably.
  • Any sign that your dog is struggling to get air.

For less dramatic changes — a mild increase in resting rate in a dog who's still alert and comfortable — a vet appointment within 24 to 48 hours is appropriate. Persistent fast breathing at rest that doesn't resolve over an hour warrants a same-day call.

What a Vet Will Do

A thorough evaluation usually includes listening to the heart and lungs with a stethoscope, chest X-rays to assess the trachea, lung fields, and heart size, and look for any fluid buildup or masses, bloodwork which may include a cardiac blood test (pro BNP), pulse ox to measure the blood oxygen level, blood pressure measurement, and sometimes an ECG (electrocardiogram) or echocardiogram (an ultrasound of the heart) to look for an arrhythmia as well as to assess the heart's structure and function.9

Treatment is directed at the underlying cause, so testing is necessary to find a diagnosis. Heart disease is managed with medications that reduce fluid buildup and support cardiac function. Respiratory infections get antimicrobials, herbal therapy, and supportive care. Laryngeal paralysis may be addressed with acupuncture or surgically. Tracheal collapse is managed with herbal therapy, cartilage support, medication, and lifestyle changes. The earlier any of these are diagnosed, the more options you have.10

Supporting Your Senior Dog at Home

Even outside of acute episodes, there's a lot you can do to make breathing easier for an aging dog:

  • Keep home comfortably cool, especially in warmer months — heat adds significant respiratory load.
  • Choose a harness over a collar to avoid pressure on the trachea, especially for small breeds prone to tracheal collapse.
  • Keep sleeping areas quiet, well-ventilated, and free from disturbance.
  • Avoid strenuous exercise and limit outings during warm or humid weather.
  • Maintaining a healthy weight — excess weight makes every breath harder.
  • Monitor resting breathing rate once a week while your dog is calm and asleep.
  • Check gum color periodically — pink and moist is normal; pale, blue, or very dry is a warning sign.
  • Reduce environmental triggers — scented candles, air fresheners, plug ins, smoke, and dusty rooms can all irritate aging airways.

A Season to Slow Down and Listen

Senior Pet Care Awareness Month is a gentle nudge to slow down and really look at the older dog in your life. Count breaths during their evening nap. Watch how they move after a walk. Listen to sounds that didn't used to be there. Notice if they're reluctant to lie flat or on their back the way they used to. These small observations, caught early, are what separate conditions that can be managed well from ones that reach crisis before anyone realizes what's happening.

Your old friend has slowed down with you over the years. If they're trying to catch their breath, they're telling you something — and the sooner you listen, the more you can do about it. Call your vet and schedule a chest X-ray and blood test. Describe what you've seen or share a video. Bring your breath-count log. For many of the conditions that cause breathing changes in senior dogs, early action is what buys more good years together on the couch, more quiet walks, and more mornings where they meet you at the door with that familiar tail wag you've loved for a decade or more.

Sources and References

  • 1,2,4,7 Comfort Paws Veterinary Care, June 26, 2026
  • 3,5,8,9 4 Paws Animal Clinic, Difficulty Breathing in Senior Dogs: When Urgent Vet Care Is Needed
  • 6,10 VSA Advanced Veterinary Care, Laryngeal Paralysis Treatment of Breathing Difficulties in Older Dogs
